Team Steins is a team of three first-year Computer Science students from Kerala, India.  Our skills are game development, web development and Python.
summary: Outpost is a story-driven mission trainer that teaches junior astronauts to run a lunar or Martian outpost. You are the commander — the fifth person in the hab, alongside an engineer, a botanist, a medic and a comms officer — and you must keep all five alive for 30 sols across 15-16 scenes. Every choice moves four meters — Oxygen, Power, Food and Morale — and every sol costs Food and Oxygen, so doing nothing is also a decision. Death is permanent, dangerous jobs only warn that someone "might get injured", and at SOL 21 Earth offers two evacuation seats for four crew: refuse the split and bring everyone home to earn the best ending, NO ONE LEFT BEHIND. Every ending closes with a debrief of what that run taught. The science is real — a 14-day lunar night, regolith shielding, solar-storm events inspired by NASA DONKI data — so players learn by consequence, not lecture. The game runs entirely in the browser: one file, no install, no server.
details:
Outpost is a story-driven mission trainer that runs entirely in the browser — one self-contained HTML file, no install, no server, works offline on a phone or a PC. Pick Moon or Mars, name your commander, and run the hab for 30 sols across 15 scenes. You are the fifth person in the hab, alongside Reyes (engineer), Anya (botanist), Kenji (medic) and Sam (comms). Every scene offers a choice, and every choice moves four meters: Oxygen, Power, Food and Morale, starting at 74, 68, 70 and 78. Every sol costs Food −1 and Oxygen −1, so doing nothing is also a decision.

Death is permanent — no load, no undo. A healthy crewmate who gets hurt becomes injured; an injured one hurt again dies. Dangerous jobs only warn that someone "might get injured" — you never see the odds. The commander can be hurt or killed only on the three "go yourself" choices, and if the commander dies the run ends as COMMAND LOST; the commander never takes an evacuation seat. At SOL 21 Earth offers two evacuation seats for four crew. Refuse the split and bring all four home to rescue at SOL 30 to earn the best ending: NO ONE LEFT BEHIND. Every ending closes with a debrief of what that run taught.

The point is to teach the hardest part of running an outpost — the decisions, not the facts. Players feel real trade-offs: spend power on shielding or risk the crew, send an injured crewmate out or go yourself, split the crew or hold together. Because the debrief names the lesson each run taught, the game works as a trainer for students, not just entertainment.

It was built with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single file, with hand-drawn SVG art, an animated vignette for every choice, and generative WebAudio sound and music — no audio files. The Moon and Mars destination images and the team photo are AI-generated; all other art is drawn in code. AI tools assisted the build and review at the team's decision; every game design decision is the team's own.

The Moon path is not a Mars copy. The same 15-scene skeleton carries different situations, risks and trade-offs: regolith shielding, a 14-day lunar night, Earth seconds away by radio instead of minutes. The gamble system hides the odds entirely — fate plays out as a struggle, never a coin flip — and the crew's thoughts, grief lines and epitaphs make every loss personal.

Real science shaped the rules. The Moon's day is 29.5 Earth days, so about 14 days of darkness make power the tightest meter on the Moon path (NASA, "To the Moon"). Piling regolith over a habitat measurably cuts radiation dose (He 2026, J. Radiol. Prot.). Solar-storm events are inspired by real NASA DONKI space-weather events, and the permanent injury rules by NASA OSDR astronaut-health research. The game pulls no live NASA feed — the values in play are simulated.
